Infinite families and sporadic solutions
of the equation φ⁡(n)=c+α​∑p|nφ⁡(p)\varphi(n)=c+\alpha\sum_{p\mid n}\varphi(p)

Hacène Belbachir ††thanks: Corresponding author. ORCID: 0000-0001-8540-3033. Affiliation: USTHB, Faculty of Mathematics, RECITS Laboratory, Affiliation: Po. Box 32 El Alia, 16111 Bab Ezzouar, Algiers, Algeria Affiliation: hacenebelbachir@gmail.com, hbelbachir@usthb.dz    Ravi Ranjan Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Central University of South Bihar, Affiliation: Gaya, Bihar 824236, India Email: raviranjan23@cusb.ac.in    Shubh N. Singh Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Central University of South Bihar, Affiliation: Gaya, Bihar 824236, India Email: shubh@cub.ac.in
October 23, 2026
Abstract

Ranjan and Singh proved that for every composite nn which is not twice an odd prime, φ⁡(n)\varphi(n) is at least one plus the sum of φ\varphi over the prime divisors of nn, with equality exactly for n=4,12,30n=4,12,30. We study the weighted equation φ⁡(n)=c+α​∑p|nφ⁡(p)\varphi(n)=c+\alpha\sum_{p\mid n}\varphi(p). We determine the parameters (c,α)(c,\alpha) admitting infinite families of solutions, prove that all remaining solutions are finite in number and arise from an explicit linear mechanism, and compute them exactly in a range of parameters; the finiteness of {4,12,30}\{4,12,30\} becomes a special case. We also settle the analogous equations for the divisor functions τ\tau and σ\sigma and for the Jordan totients, and, from known results on the sum of the prime divisors, derive the full asymptotic expansion of the average deficiency. In the range |c|≤10|c|\leq 10, 1≤α≤61\leq\alpha\leq 6 the composite solution set is determined completely, and the number and the size of the sporadic solutions are shown to be bounded by polynomials in |c|+α|c|+\alpha. Finally, replacing the prime values φ⁡(p)\varphi(p) by their iterates φ(k)​(p)\varphi^{(k)}(p), we determine all solutions of φ⁡(n)=1+∑p|nφ(k)​(p)\varphi(n)=1+\sum_{p\mid n}\varphi^{(k)}(p): the solution sets are {1,4,12,30}\{1,4,12,30\}, {1,3,4,10}\{1,3,4,10\} and, for every k≥3k\geq 3, {1,3,4}\{1,3,4\}; for the weighted iterated equation we exhibit an infinite family governed by the safe primes.

2020 MSC: 11A25 (primary); 11N37 (secondary).
Keywords: Euler’s totient function, divisor functions, Jordan totient, prime–composite characterizations, average orders, iterated totient.

1 Introduction

Euler’s totient function φ⁡(n)\varphi(n) counts the positive integers up to nn that are coprime to nn. Like most multiplicative functions its behaviour is governed by the prime factorization of the argument, and a recurring theme in elementary number theory is the classification of the integers at which an arithmetic identity, generically true for primes or generically failing for composites, admits exceptional solutions. The prototype is Lehmer’s still-open problem [8] of whether φ⁡(n)|n−1\varphi(n)\mid n-1 can hold for composite nn; a solved relative is Subbarao’s theorem [10] that his primality congruence admits exactly the composite solutions n∈{4,6,22}n\in\{4,6,22\}.

Ranjan and Singh [9] recently added a new instance to this family. Observing that

φ⁡(4)=1+φ⁡(2),φ⁡(12)=1+φ⁡(2)+φ⁡(3),φ⁡(30)=1+φ⁡(2)+φ⁡(3)+φ⁡(5),\varphi(4)=1+\varphi(2),\qquad\varphi(12)=1+\varphi(2)+\varphi(3),\qquad\varphi(30)=1+\varphi(2)+\varphi(3)+\varphi(5),

they asked for which composite numbers such an identity can hold and proved:

Theorem 1.1 (Ranjan–Singh [9]).

Let nn be a composite number which is not twice an odd prime, and let p1,…,prp_{1},\dots,p_{r} be its distinct prime divisors. Then

φ⁡(n)≥ 1+∑i=1rφ⁡(pi),\varphi(n)\;\geq\;1+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\varphi(p_{i}), (1)

with equality if and only if n∈{4,12,30}n\in\{4,12,30\}. Moreover φ⁡(2​p)<1+φ⁡(2)+φ⁡(p)\varphi(2p)<1+\varphi(2)+\varphi(p) for every odd prime pp.

Their proof rests on two elementary product–sum inequalities borrowed from Ecker [5]: a​b≥a+bab\geq a+b for a,b≥2a,b\geq 2 (equality if and only if a=b=2a=b=2), and a1⋯am>a1+⋯+ama_{1}\cdots a_{m}>a_{1}+\cdots+a_{m} whenever 2≤a1≤⋯≤am2\leq a_{1}\leq\cdots\leq a_{m} and m≥3m\geq 3.

The purpose of the present paper is fourfold. First (§3) we treat the analogous equation

f⁡(n)= 1+∑p|nf⁡(p)f(n)\;=\;1+\sum_{p\mid n}f(p) (2)

for the divisor-count function τ\tau, the sum-of-divisors function σ\sigma, and the Jordan totients JkJ_{k}, obtaining in each case a complete answer. The outcomes are strikingly different from one function to the next: for τ\tau the composite solution set is the infinite family {p2:p​ prime}\{p^{2}:p\text{ prime}\}; for σ\sigma and for JkJ_{k} (k≥2k\geq 2) it is empty; for φ\varphi it is the finite set {4,12,30}\{4,12,30\}. Second (§4–§5) we study weighted and simultaneous versions of (2), where parity constraints, an exact classification of the infinite solution families, and a finiteness theorem give a complete structure theory — from which the finiteness of the Ranjan–Singh exceptional set follows as a corollary; in the range |c|≤10|c|\leq 10, 1≤α≤61\leq\alpha\leq 6 the solution sets are then computed completely, and uniform polynomial bounds in |c|+α|c|+\alpha are proved. Third (§6) we measure how far a typical integer is from satisfying (1): a simple identity reduces the average deficiency to classical results of Alladi–Erdős and De Koninck–Ivić, which yields its full asymptotic expansion. Fourth (§7) we replace the prime values φ⁡(p)\varphi(p) in (1) by their iterates φ(k)​(p)\varphi^{(k)}(p) and determine all solutions for every k≥1k\geq 1: the monotonicity of the iterates reduces each case to Theorem 1.1, and the solution sets stabilise at {1,3,4}\{1,3,4\} for all k≥3k\geq 3.

2 Notation and preliminaries

Throughout, n=p1a1⋯prarn=p_{1}^{a_{1}}\cdots p_{r}^{a_{r}} denotes the canonical factorization of an integer n≥2n\geq 2, with p1<⋯<prp_{1}<\cdots<p_{r}, and ω⁡(n)=r\omega(n)=r is the number of distinct prime divisors of nn. We write τ⁡(n)=∑d|n1\tau(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}1, σ⁡(n)=∑d|nd\sigma(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d, and for k≥1k\geq 1

Jk​(n)=nk​∏p|n(1−1pk),J_{k}(n)\;=\;n^{k}\prod_{p\mid n}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{p^{k}}\Bigr),

the Jordan totient, so that J1=φJ_{1}=\varphi and Jk​(pa)=pk⁡(a−1)​(pk−1)J_{k}(p^{a})=p^{k(a-1)}(p^{k}-1) [11]. All three of φ,τ,σ\varphi,\tau,\sigma and every JkJ_{k} are multiplicative. On primes,

φ⁡(p)=p−1,τ⁡(p)=2,σ⁡(p)=p+1,Jk​(p)=pk−1.\varphi(p)=p-1,\qquad\tau(p)=2,\qquad\sigma(p)=p+1,\qquad J_{k}(p)=p^{k}-1.

We shall use the elementary fact that φ⁡(n)\varphi(n) is even for every n≥3n\geq 3, the fact that φ⁡(n)=n−1\varphi(n)=n-1 if and only if nn is prime, and the bound φ⁡(n)≤n/2\varphi(n)\leq n/2 for even nn. For k≥1k\geq 1, φ(k)\varphi^{(k)} denotes the kk-fold iterate of φ\varphi, with φ(1)=φ\varphi^{(1)}=\varphi.

3 The equation f⁡(n)=1+∑p|nf⁡(p)f(n)=1+\sum_{p\mid n}f(p) for τ\tau, σ\sigma and JkJ_{k}

3.1 The divisor-count function

Since τ⁡(p)=2\tau(p)=2, equation (2) for f=τf=\tau reads τ⁡(n)=1+2​ω​(n)\tau(n)=1+2\,\omega(n).

Theorem 3.1.

A composite number nn satisfies τ⁡(n)=1+∑p|nτ⁡(p)\tau(n)=1+\sum_{p\mid n}\tau(p) if and only if n=p2n=p^{2} for some prime pp.

Proof.

If n=pan=p^{a} is a prime power, the equation reads a+1=3a+1=3, i.e. a=2a=2; every n=p2n=p^{2} is a solution and no other prime power is.

Suppose now ω⁡(n)=r≥2\omega(n)=r\geq 2. Since each exponent satisfies ai+1≥2a_{i}+1\geq 2,

τ⁡(n)=∏i=1r(ai+1)≥ 2r.\tau(n)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}(a_{i}+1)\;\geq\;2^{r}.

For r≥3r\geq 3 we get τ⁡(n)≥2r>1+2​r\tau(n)\geq 2^{r}>1+2r, because 2r−2​r−12^{r}-2r-1 is positive at r=3r=3 and increasing; hence no solutions. For r=2r=2 the equation demands τ⁡(n)=5\tau(n)=5, a prime value of τ\tau; but τ⁡(n)=(a1+1)​(a2+1)\tau(n)=(a_{1}+1)(a_{2}+1) with both factors ≥2\geq 2 is composite. No solutions exist with r=2r=2, which completes the proof. ∎

Thus, in contrast with the finite exceptional set {4,12,30}\{4,12,30\} of Theorem 1.1, the τ\tau-analogue possesses the infinite solution family {4,9,25,49,121,…}\{4,9,25,49,121,\dots\} (the squares of primes, OEIS A001248).

3.2 The sum-of-divisors function

For f=σf=\sigma the outcome is the opposite extreme: the analogue of (1) holds strictly for every composite number, with no exceptional set whatsoever.

Theorem 3.2.

For every composite nn,

σ⁡(n)> 1+∑p|nσ⁡(p),\sigma(n)\;>\;1+\sum_{p\mid n}\sigma(p),

and consequently the equation σ⁡(n)=1+∑p|nσ⁡(p)\sigma(n)=1+\sum_{p\mid n}\sigma(p) has no composite solution.

Proof.

Because nn is composite, the integers 1,p1,…,pr,n1,\,p_{1},\dots,p_{r},\,n are pairwise distinct divisors of nn; hence

σ⁡(n)≥ 1+∑i=1rpi+n.\sigma(n)\;\geq\;1+\sum_{i=1}^{r}p_{i}+n.

On the other hand 1+∑p|nσ⁡(p)=1+∑i=1r(pi+1)=1+r+∑i=1rpi1+\sum_{p\mid n}\sigma(p)=1+\sum_{i=1}^{r}(p_{i}+1)=1+r+\sum_{i=1}^{r}p_{i}. Subtracting,

σ⁡(n)−(1+∑p|nσ⁡(p))≥n−r=n−ω⁡(n)> 0,\sigma(n)-\Bigl(1+\sum_{p\mid n}\sigma(p)\Bigr)\;\geq\;n-r\;=\;n-\omega(n)\;>\;0,

since ω⁡(n)≤log2⁡n<n\omega(n)\leq\log_{2}n<n for all n≥2n\geq 2. ∎

3.3 Jordan totients of order k≥2k\geq 2

For the higher Jordan totients the left-hand side of (2) grows polynomially in nn while the right-hand side grows only with the prime support, and again no composite solutions survive.

Theorem 3.3.

Let k≥2k\geq 2. For every composite nn,

Jk​(n)> 1+∑p|nJk​(p),J_{k}(n)\;>\;1+\sum_{p\mid n}J_{k}(p),

so the equation Jk​(n)=1+∑p|nJk​(p)J_{k}(n)=1+\sum_{p\mid n}J_{k}(p) has no composite solution.

Proof.

Put xi=pik−1=Jk​(pi)x_{i}=p_{i}^{k}-1=J_{k}(p_{i}) and note xi≥2k−1≥3x_{i}\geq 2^{k}-1\geq 3 for k≥2k\geq 2.

If n=pan=p^{a} with a≥2a\geq 2, then Jk​(n)=pk⁡(a−1)​(pk−1)≥pk​(pk−1)>1+(pk−1)=pkJ_{k}(n)=p^{k(a-1)}(p^{k}-1)\geq p^{k}(p^{k}-1)>1+(p^{k}-1)=p^{k}, the last inequality because pk−1≥3p^{k}-1\geq 3 implies pk​(pk−1)≥3​pk>pkp^{k}(p^{k}-1)\geq 3p^{k}>p^{k}.

If r≥2r\geq 2, then by multiplicativity Jk​(n)≥∏i=1rxiJ_{k}(n)\geq\prod_{i=1}^{r}x_{i}, and it suffices to prove

∏i=1rxi> 1+∑i=1rxi(xi≥3,r≥2).\prod_{i=1}^{r}x_{i}\;>\;1+\sum_{i=1}^{r}x_{i}\qquad(x_{i}\geq 3,\ r\geq 2). (3)

For r=2r=2: (x1−1)​(x2−1)≥4>2(x_{1}-1)(x_{2}-1)\geq 4>2, which rearranges to x1​x2>1+x1+x2x_{1}x_{2}>1+x_{1}+x_{2}. For r≥3r\geq 3, induction: if (3) holds for r−1r-1 terms, then ∏i≤rxi>xr​(1+∑i<rxi)≥xr+3​∑i<rxi>1+∑i≤rxi\prod_{i\leq r}x_{i}>x_{r}\bigl(1+\sum_{i<r}x_{i}\bigr)\geq x_{r}+3\sum_{i<r}x_{i}>1+\sum_{i\leq r}x_{i}. ∎

Remark 3.4.

The three theorems above, together with Theorem 1.1, exhibit the full spectrum of behaviours of equation (2) within one natural family of multiplicative functions: an infinite solution set (τ\tau), a finite nonempty one (φ\varphi), and empty ones (σ\sigma, all JkJ_{k} with k≥2k\geq 2). Heuristically, the size of the solution set is governed by the growth of f⁡(pa)f(p^{a}) against f⁡(p)f(p): the slower the growth, the richer the solution set.

4 The weighted equation: a complete structure theory

Consider, for integer parameters cc and α≥1\alpha\geq 1, the weighted equation

φ⁡(n)=c+α​∑p|nφ⁡(p),\varphi(n)\;=\;c+\alpha\sum_{p\mid n}\varphi(p), (4)

of which Theorem 1.1 is the case (c,α)=(1,1)(c,\alpha)=(1,1). Write Sm:=∑q|mφ⁡(q)S_{m}:=\sum_{q\mid m}\varphi(q) for the prime-support sum, so that (4) reads φ⁡(n)=c+α​Sn\varphi(n)=c+\alpha S_{n}. In this section we determine the structure of the composite solution set of (4) completely: parity constraints (Theorem 4.1), an exact classification of the infinite families (Theorem 4.2), and a finiteness theorem for what remains (Theorem 4.4). The structure theorem is then made completely explicit in the range |c|≤10|c|\leq 10, 1≤α≤61\leq\alpha\leq 6 (Theorem 4.12), and uniform polynomial bounds in |c|+α|c|+\alpha are derived from it (Theorem 4.13).

4.1 Parity constraints

Theorem 4.1 (Parity constraints).

Let n≥4n\geq 4 be a composite solution of (4). Then: (i) if cc is odd and α\alpha is even, no such nn exists; (ii) if cc and α\alpha are both odd, nn is even; (iii) if cc is even and α\alpha is odd, nn is odd; (iv) if cc and α\alpha are both even, no parity restriction holds.

Proof.

For n≥3n\geq 3 the value φ⁡(n)\varphi(n) is even. On the other side, φ⁡(2)=1\varphi(2)=1 is the only odd value of φ\varphi at a prime, whence Sn≡𝟏2|n(mod2)S_{n}\equiv\mathbf{1}_{2\mid n}\pmod{2} and the right-hand side of (4) is congruent to c+α​ 12|nc+\alpha\,\mathbf{1}_{2\mid n} modulo 22. Requiring it to be even yields exactly the four cases. Case (iv) is realized: (c,α)=(2,2)(c,\alpha)=(2,2) has both the even solution 88 and the odd solution 99. ∎

4.2 Classification of the infinite families

The exclusion of n=2​pn=2p in Theorem 1.1 is not an accident of the proof: the integers 2​p2p form an exact infinite family for the neighbouring pair (c,α)=(−1,1)(c,\alpha)=(-1,1), since φ⁡(2​p)=p−1=S2​p−1\varphi(2p)=p-1=S_{2p}-1. This phenomenon is completely general.

Theorem 4.2 (Infinite families).

Let m≥2m\geq 2 be fixed. Every integer n=m​pn=mp, with pp prime and p∤mp\nmid m, satisfies (4) if and only if

α=φ⁡(m)andc=−φ⁡(m)​Sm.\alpha=\varphi(m)\qquad\text{and}\qquad c=-\varphi(m)\,S_{m}.

We call such a pair (c,α)(c,\alpha) matched, with modulus mm. For each α\alpha there are only finitely many matched moduli, since φ⁡(m)=α\varphi(m)=\alpha has finitely many solutions mm.

Proof.

For p∤mp\nmid m, multiplicativity gives φ⁡(m​p)=φ⁡(m)​(p−1)\varphi(mp)=\varphi(m)(p-1) and Sm​p=Sm+p−1S_{mp}=S_{m}+p-1. Equation (4) becomes the identity in pp

φ⁡(m)​(p−1)=c+α​Sm+α⁡(p−1),\varphi(m)(p-1)\;=\;c+\alpha S_{m}+\alpha(p-1),

which holds for infinitely many (equivalently, for all admissible) primes pp if and only if the coefficients of p−1p-1 and the constant terms match: φ⁡(m)=α\varphi(m)=\alpha and c+α​Sm=0c+\alpha S_{m}=0. ∎

For example, the matched pairs in the range |c|≤10|c|\leq 10, 1≤α≤61\leq\alpha\leq 6 are

m(c,α)family2(−1,1){2​p}4(−2,2){4​p}3(−4,2){3​p}6(−6,2){6​p}8(−4,4){8​p}\begin{array}[]{c|c|c}m&(c,\alpha)&\text{family}\\ \hline\cr 2&(-1,1)&\{2p\}\\ 4&(-2,2)&\{4p\}\\ 3&(-4,2)&\{3p\}\\ 6&(-6,2)&\{6p\}\\ 8&(-4,4)&\{8p\}\end{array}

and the pair (1,1)(1,1) of Theorem 1.1 is unmatched: φ⁡(m)=1\varphi(m)=1 forces m=2m=2, which would require c=−1≠1c=-1\neq 1.

4.3 Finiteness outside the families, and the sporadic mechanism

Lemma 4.3.

Let nn be a composite solution of (4), let PP be the largest prime factor of nn and write n=m′​Pan=m^{\prime}P^{a} with P∤m′P\nmid m^{\prime}, a≥1a\geq 1. If a=1a=1 then

(φ⁡(m′)−α)​(P−1)=c+α​Sm′,\bigl(\varphi(m^{\prime})-\alpha\bigr)(P-1)\;=\;c+\alpha S_{m^{\prime}}, (5)

while if a≥2a\geq 2 then (P−1)​(φ⁡(m′)​Pa−1−α)=c+α​Sm′(P-1)\bigl(\varphi(m^{\prime})P^{a-1}-\alpha\bigr)=c+\alpha S_{m^{\prime}}.

Proof.

Immediate from φ⁡(n)=φ⁡(m′)​Pa−1​(P−1)\varphi(n)=\varphi(m^{\prime})P^{a-1}(P-1) and Sn=Sm′+P−1S_{n}=S_{m^{\prime}}+P-1. ∎

Equation (5) is the engine of the whole subject. When m′m^{\prime} is a matched modulus both sides vanish and PP is unconstrained: this reproduces the infinite families. Otherwise PP is determined by m′m^{\prime}, and the point of the next theorem is that only finitely many m′m^{\prime} can produce a legitimate PP.

Theorem 4.4 (Structure theorem).

For every pair (c,α)(c,\alpha), the set of composite solutions of (4) is the union of the families {mp:pprime,p∤m}\{mp:p\ \text{prime},\,p\nmid m\} over the finitely many matched moduli mm, together with a finite sporadic set F⁡(c,α)F(c,\alpha). In particular, if (c,α)(c,\alpha) is unmatched —as is (1,1)(1,1)— the composite solution set is finite.

Proof.

Let n=m′​Pan=m^{\prime}P^{a} be a solution as in Lemma 4.3 which does not belong to a matched family. We use the elementary bounds φ⁡(m)≥m/2\varphi(m)\geq\sqrt{m/2} and ω⁡(m)≤log2⁡m\omega(m)\leq\log_{2}m, and we note that PP exceeds every prime factor of m′m^{\prime} (being the largest prime factor of nn, and coprime to m′m^{\prime}); thus, with QQ the largest prime factor of m′m^{\prime} (set Q=1Q=1 if m′=1m^{\prime}=1), we have P≥Q+1P\geq Q+1 and Sm′≤ω⁡(m′)​(Q−1)S_{m^{\prime}}\leq\omega(m^{\prime})(Q-1).

Case a=1a=1. If φ⁡(m′)=α\varphi(m^{\prime})=\alpha then, m′m^{\prime} being unmatched, c+α​Sm′≠0c+\alpha S_{m^{\prime}}\neq 0 and (5) is contradictory; besides, φ⁡(m′)=α\varphi(m^{\prime})=\alpha already confines m′m^{\prime} to a finite set. So assume φ⁡(m′)≠α\varphi(m^{\prime})\neq\alpha; then (5) determines P−1=(c+α​Sm′)/(φ⁡(m′)−α)P-1=(c+\alpha S_{m^{\prime}})/(\varphi(m^{\prime})-\alpha), at most one prime for each m′m^{\prime}. If moreover φ⁡(m′)>α\varphi(m^{\prime})>\alpha, the requirement P−1≥QP-1\geq Q forces

Q≤|c|+α​ω​(m′)​(Q−1)φ⁡(m′)−α,henceφ⁡(m′)<α+|c|+α​ω​(m′)≤α+|c|+α​log2​m′.Q\;\leq\;\frac{|c|+\alpha\,\omega(m^{\prime})(Q-1)}{\varphi(m^{\prime})-\alpha},\qquad\text{hence}\qquad\varphi(m^{\prime})\;<\;\alpha+|c|+\alpha\,\omega(m^{\prime})\;\leq\;\alpha+|c|+\alpha\log_{2}m^{\prime}.

Since φ⁡(m′)≥m′/2\varphi(m^{\prime})\geq\sqrt{m^{\prime}/2} grows faster than log2⁡m′\log_{2}m^{\prime}, only finitely many m′m^{\prime} qualify; the finitely many m′m^{\prime} with φ⁡(m′)<α\varphi(m^{\prime})<\alpha are handled trivially. Each surviving m′m^{\prime} contributes at most one solution.

Case a≥2a\geq 2. Here (P−1)​(φ⁡(m′)​Pa−1−α)=c+α​Sm′(P-1)\bigl(\varphi(m^{\prime})P^{a-1}-\alpha\bigr)=c+\alpha S_{m^{\prime}}. If the second factor is nonpositive, then φ⁡(m′)​Pa−1≤α\varphi(m^{\prime})P^{a-1}\leq\alpha, which bounds m′m^{\prime}, PP and aa. Otherwise it is at least 11, and since Sm′≤ω⁡(m′)​(Q−1)≤ω⁡(m′)​(P−1)S_{m^{\prime}}\leq\omega(m^{\prime})(Q-1)\leq\omega(m^{\prime})(P-1), dividing by P−1P-1 gives

φ⁡(m′)​Pa−1≤α+|c|+α​ω​(m′)≤α+|c|+α​log2​m′.\varphi(m^{\prime})P^{a-1}\;\leq\;\alpha+|c|+\alpha\,\omega(m^{\prime})\;\leq\;\alpha+|c|+\alpha\log_{2}m^{\prime}.

As φ⁡(m′)≥m′/2\varphi(m^{\prime})\geq\sqrt{m^{\prime}/2}, this bounds m′m^{\prime}, then Pa−1P^{a-1}, hence PP and aa. In all cases only finitely many solutions arise. ∎

Corollary 4.5.

The finiteness of the exceptional set in Theorem 1.1 is a special case of Theorem 4.4: the pair (1,1)(1,1) is unmatched, and its sporadic set is F⁡(1,1)={4,12,30}F(1,1)=\{4,12,30\}. The elements 1212 and 3030 arise from (5): for n=12=4⋅3n=12=4\cdot 3, (φ⁡(4)−1)​(3−1)=2=1+S4(\varphi(4)-1)(3-1)=2=1+S_{4}, and for n=30=6⋅5n=30=6\cdot 5, (φ⁡(6)−1)​(5−1)=4=1+S6(\varphi(6)-1)(5-1)=4=1+S_{6}; the element 4=224=2^{2} arises from the case a≥2a\geq 2 of Lemma 4.3, with m′=1m^{\prime}=1: (2−1)​(1⋅2−1)=1=1+S1(2-1)(1\cdot 2-1)=1=1+S_{1}.

Corollary 4.6.

If cc is odd and α\alpha is even —for instance (c,α)=(1,2)(c,\alpha)=(1,2)— equation (4) has no composite solution at all (Theorem 4.1(i)).

4.4 Exact determination of the sporadic sets

Theorem 4.4 is effective, and for the five matched pairs above the bounds are small enough to compute the sporadic sets exactly.

Lemma 4.7 (Explicit bounds).

Let (c,α)(c,\alpha) be one of the five matched pairs (so |c|≤6|c|\leq 6, α≤4\alpha\leq 4), and let n=m′​Pan=m^{\prime}P^{a} be a sporadic composite solution, decomposed as in Lemma 4.3. Then ω⁡(m′)≤3\omega(m^{\prime})\leq 3 and φ⁡(m′)≤18\varphi(m^{\prime})\leq 18, hence m′≤648m^{\prime}\leq 648; moreover P≤83P\leq 83 and a≤5a\leq 5.

Proof.

Corollary 4.14.
  1. (i)

    If α≥3\alpha\geq 3 is odd, there is no matched modulus, and for every cc the composite solution set of (4) is finite, of cardinality ≪(|c|+α)2​log2⁡(|c|+α)\ll(|c|+\alpha)^{2}\log^{2}(|c|+\alpha).

  2. (ii)

    For α=1\alpha=1 and c≤0c\leq 0 one has F⁡(c,1)=∅F(c,1)=\varnothing: the equation φ⁡(n)=c+Sn\varphi(n)=c+S_{n} has composite solutions only for c=−1c=-1 (the family 2​p2p) and for c≥1c\geq 1.

Proof.

(i) A matched modulus mm satisfies φ⁡(m)=α\varphi(m)=\alpha, which is impossible for odd α≥3\alpha\geq 3 since φ⁡(m)\varphi(m) is even for m≥3m\geq 3 and φ⁡(1)=φ⁡(2)=1\varphi(1)=\varphi(2)=1; Theorem 4.13 then bounds the whole solution set. (ii) If nn is composite and not twice an odd prime, Theorem 1.1 gives φ⁡(n)≥1+Sn>c+Sn\varphi(n)\geq 1+S_{n}>c+S_{n} for c≤0c\leq 0; if n=2​pn=2p then φ⁡(n)=Sn−1\varphi(n)=S_{n}-1, so c=−1c=-1 and nn belongs to the matched family. ∎

4.7 Numerical census

An exhaustive direct scan over composites n≤2⋅105n\leq 2\cdot 10^{5} and weights |c|≤10|c|\leq 10, 1≤α≤61\leq\alpha\leq 6 agrees with Theorems 4.2 and 4.8 in every case, and shows in addition that all unmatched pairs in the range have at most nine composite solutions up to 2⋅1052\cdot 10^{5}; a small sample:

(c,α)composite solutions ​n≤2⋅105(1,1)4, 12, 30(0,2)4, 18(2,2)8, 9, 24, 60, 70(0,4)8, 36, 45, 50, 91, 105, 126(6,6)27, 49, 72, 112, 180, 312, 380, 418, 462\begin{array}[]{c|l}(c,\alpha)&\text{composite solutions }n\leq 2\cdot 10^{5}\\ \hline\cr(1,1)&4,\ 12,\ 30\\ (0,2)&4,\ 18\\ (2,2)&8,\ 9,\ 24,\ 60,\ 70\\ (0,4)&8,\ 36,\ 45,\ 50,\ 91,\ 105,\ 126\\ (6,6)&27,\ 49,\ 72,\ 112,\ 180,\ 312,\ 380,\ 418,\ 462\end{array}

The parity constraints are visible throughout: every solution found for (3,3)(3,3) is even and every solution for (0,3)(0,3) is odd, in accordance with Theorem 4.1.

5 Simultaneous equations

Write (Eφ)(E_{\varphi}), (Eτ)(E_{\tau}), (Eσ)(E_{\sigma}) for equation (2) with f=φ,τ,σf=\varphi,\tau,\sigma respectively. Combining Theorems 1.1, 3.1 and 3.2 yields complete answers for all conjunctions.

Theorem 5.1.

(i) The unique composite integer satisfying (Eφ)(E_{\varphi}) and (Eτ)(E_{\tau}) simultaneously is n=4n=4. (ii) No integer n≥2n\geq 2 satisfies (Eφ)(E_{\varphi}), (Eτ)(E_{\tau}) and (Eσ)(E_{\sigma}) simultaneously; indeed already (Eσ)(E_{\sigma}) alone has no composite solution, and no prime satisfies (Eτ)(E_{\tau}).

Proof.

(i) By Theorems 1.1 and 3.1 the composite solutions of (Eφ)(E_{\varphi}) are {4,12,30}\{4,12,30\} and those of (Eτ)(E_{\tau}) are the prime squares; the intersection is {4}\{4\}, since neither 1212 nor 3030 is the square of a prime. One checks directly: φ⁡(4)=2=1+φ⁡(2)\varphi(4)=2=1+\varphi(2) and τ⁡(4)=3=1+τ⁡(2)\tau(4)=3=1+\tau(2).

(ii) For a prime pp, (Eτ)(E_{\tau}) reads 2=32=3, false; combined with Theorem 3.2 for composites this settles the claim. ∎

Thus, imposing several of these equations at once collapses the solution set, first to {4}\{4\} and then to ∅\varnothing.

6 The average size of the deficiency

Theorem 1.1 says that the deficiency

Δ⁡(n):=φ⁡(n)−1−∑p|nφ⁡(p)\Delta(n)\;:=\;\varphi(n)-1-\sum_{p\mid n}\varphi(p)

is nonnegative for composite n≠2​pn\neq 2p and vanishes only thrice. How large is it on average? The answer is: as large as φ\varphi itself, the subtracted term being negligible at the scale x2x^{2}.

Theorem 6.1.

Let Aj=(−1)j−1​dj−1d​sj−1​(ζ⁡(s)s)|s=2A_{j}=(-1)^{j-1}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^{j-1}}{\mathrm{d}s^{j-1}}\Bigl(\dfrac{\zeta(s)}{s}\Bigr)\Big|_{s=2}, so that A1=π212A_{1}=\dfrac{\pi^{2}}{12} and A2=ζ⁡(2)4−ζ′​(2)2A_{2}=\dfrac{\zeta(2)}{4}-\dfrac{\zeta^{\prime}(2)}{2}. For every fixed M≥1M\geq 1,

∑n≤xΔ⁡(n)=3π2​x2−∑j=1MAj​x2logj⁡x+O⁡(x2logM+1⁡x).\sum_{n\leq x}\Delta(n)\;=\;\frac{3}{\pi^{2}}\,x^{2}\;-\;\sum_{j=1}^{M}A_{j}\,\frac{x^{2}}{\log^{j}x}\;+\;O\!\left(\frac{x^{2}}{\log^{M+1}x}\right).

In particular the mean value 1x​∑n≤xΔ⁡(n)∼3π2​x\frac{1}{x}\sum_{n\leq x}\Delta(n)\sim\frac{3}{\pi^{2}}x.

Proof.

Since φ⁡(p)=p−1\varphi(p)=p-1, we have ∑p|nφ⁡(p)=β⁡(n)−ω⁡(n)\sum_{p\mid n}\varphi(p)=\beta(n)-\omega(n), where β⁡(n)=∑p|np\beta(n)=\sum_{p\mid n}p is the sum of the distinct prime divisors of nn. Hence

∑n≤xΔ⁡(n)=∑n≤xφ⁡(n)−⌊x⌋−∑n≤xβ⁡(n)+∑n≤xω⁡(n).\sum_{n\leq x}\Delta(n)\;=\;\sum_{n\leq x}\varphi(n)\;-\;\lfloor x\rfloor\;-\;\sum_{n\leq x}\beta(n)\;+\;\sum_{n\leq x}\omega(n).

The first sum equals 3π2​x2+O⁡(x​log⁡x)\frac{3}{\pi^{2}}x^{2}+O(x\log x) [7, Th. 330], and the last one is O⁡(x​log⁡log​x)O(x\log\log x) [7, Th. 430]. The leading term of ∑n≤xβ⁡(n)\sum_{n\leq x}\beta(n), namely π212​x2/log⁡x\frac{\pi^{2}}{12}x^{2}/\log x, is due to Alladi and Erdős [3], and the full expansion ∑n≤xβ⁡(n)=∑j=1MAj​x2/logj⁡x+O⁡(x2/logM+1⁡x)\sum_{n\leq x}\beta(n)=\sum_{j=1}^{M}A_{j}x^{2}/\log^{j}x+O(x^{2}/\log^{M+1}x) to De Koninck and Ivić [4]. Combining these estimates proves the theorem. ∎

Remark 6.2.

The leading term also follows from the exact identity ∑n≤x∑p|nφ⁡(p)=∑k≥1P⁡(x/k)\sum_{n\leq x}\sum_{p\mid n}\varphi(p)=\sum_{k\geq 1}P(x/k), where P⁡(y)=∑p≤y(p−1)P(y)=\sum_{p\leq y}(p-1), together with the prime number theorem. Numerically, (∑n≤x∑p|nφ⁡(p))​log⁡x/x2\bigl(\sum_{n\leq x}\sum_{p\mid n}\varphi(p)\bigr)\log x/x^{2} equals 0.91530.9153, 0.89780.8978, 0.88580.8858 at x=105,106,107x=10^{5},10^{6},10^{7} (exact sieve computations), whereas the expansion ∑j≤MAj/logj−1⁡x\sum_{j\leq M}A_{j}/\log^{j-1}x truncated at M=2M=2 gives 0.89890.8989, 0.88620.8862, 0.87710.8771 and at M=3M=3 reduces the discrepancy at x=107x=10^{7} to 0.2%0.2\%.

7 Iterated totients on the prime divisors

In this section we replace the prime values φ⁡(p)\varphi(p) in (1) by their iterates and determine, for every k≥1k\geq 1, all positive integers nn with

φ⁡(n)= 1+∑p|nφ(k)​(p).\varphi(n)\;=\;1+\sum_{p\mid n}\varphi^{(k)}(p). (7)

The answer rests on Theorem 1.1 and on the following monotonicity.

Lemma 7.1.

For every n≥1n\geq 1 the sequence (φ(j)​(n))j≥1\bigl(\varphi^{(j)}(n)\bigr)_{j\geq 1} is non-increasing. Moreover, for every prime p≥3p\geq 3 and every k≥2k\geq 2, φ(k)​(p)≤φ⁡(p−1)≤p−12\varphi^{(k)}(p)\leq\varphi(p-1)\leq\frac{p-1}{2}.

Proof.

Since φ⁡(m)≤m\varphi(m)\leq m for all m≥1m\geq 1, we have φ(j+1)​(n)=φ⁡(φ(j)​(n))≤φ(j)​(n)\varphi^{(j+1)}(n)=\varphi\bigl(\varphi^{(j)}(n)\bigr)\leq\varphi^{(j)}(n). For p≥3p\geq 3 prime, φ(2)​(p)=φ⁡(p−1)\varphi^{(2)}(p)=\varphi(p-1) and p−1p-1 is even, so φ⁡(p−1)≤(p−1)/2\varphi(p-1)\leq(p-1)/2; the first part gives φ(k)​(p)≤φ(2)​(p)\varphi^{(k)}(p)\leq\varphi^{(2)}(p) for k≥2k\geq 2. ∎

Write X:={1,2,4,12,30}∪{p, 2p:podd prime}X:=\{1,2,4,12,30\}\cup\{p,\,2p:\ p\ \text{odd prime}\}. For n∉Xn\notin X, nn is composite and not twice an odd prime, and n∉{4,12,30}n\notin\{4,12,30\}; hence Theorem 1.1 gives φ⁡(n)>1+∑p|nφ⁡(p)≥1+∑p|nφ(k)​(p)\varphi(n)>1+\sum_{p\mid n}\varphi(p)\geq 1+\sum_{p\mid n}\varphi^{(k)}(p) by Lemma 7.1. Thus, for every k≥1k\geq 1, every solution of (7) lies in XX, and it remains to examine the elements of XX.

Theorem 7.2.

The solutions of (7) are exactly:

  1. (i)

    n∈{1,4,12,30}n\in\{1,4,12,30\} if k=1k=1;

  2. (ii)

    n∈{1,3,4,10}n\in\{1,3,4,10\} if k=2k=2;

  3. (iii)

    n∈{1,3,4}n\in\{1,3,4\} if k≥3k\geq 3.

Proof.

The values involved are collected in the following table, where the right-hand side of (7) is denoted Rk​(n)R_{k}(n):

nφ⁡(n)R1​(n)R2​(n)Rk​(n),k≥31111121222422221244333088543232262433104643\begin{array}[]{c|c|c|c|c}n&\varphi(n)&R_{1}(n)&R_{2}(n)&R_{k}(n),\ k\geq 3\\ \hline\cr 1&1&1&1&1\\ 2&1&2&2&2\\ 4&2&2&2&2\\ 12&4&4&3&3\\ 30&8&8&5&4\\ 3&2&3&2&2\\ 6&2&4&3&3\\ 10&4&6&4&3\end{array}

(For n=1n=1 the sum is empty. For k≥3k\geq 3, φ(k)​(2)=φ(k)​(3)=1\varphi^{(k)}(2)=\varphi^{(k)}(3)=1 and φ(k)​(5)=1\varphi^{(k)}(5)=1.) This settles n∈{1,2,4,12,30}n\in\{1,2,4,12,30\} for all kk, and n∈{6,10}n\in\{6,10\} once these are shown to be the only candidates among the 2​p2p.

Case k=1k=1. For an odd prime pp, φ⁡(p)=p−1<p=R1​(p)\varphi(p)=p-1<p=R_{1}(p), and φ⁡(2​p)=p−1<p+1=R1​(2​p)\varphi(2p)=p-1<p+1=R_{1}(2p). With the table, the solutions are {1,4,12,30}\{1,4,12,30\}.

Odd primes, k≥2k\geq 2. Let n=pn=p be an odd prime. For k=2k=2, (7) reads p−1=1+φ⁡(p−1)p-1=1+\varphi(p-1), i.e. φ⁡(p−1)=p−2\varphi(p-1)=p-2, which forces p−1p-1 to be prime; p−1p-1 and pp being consecutive primes, p=3p=3. For k≥3k\geq 3, Lemma 7.1 gives p−1=1+φ(k)​(p)≤1+p−12p-1=1+\varphi^{(k)}(p)\leq 1+\frac{p-1}{2}, hence p≤3p\leq 3, and p=3p=3 is a solution by the table.

Twice an odd prime, k≥2k\geq 2. Let n=2​pn=2p with pp an odd prime, so φ⁡(n)=p−1\varphi(n)=p-1 and Rk​(2​p)=1+φ(k)​(2)+φ(k)​(p)=2+φ(k)​(p)R_{k}(2p)=1+\varphi^{(k)}(2)+\varphi^{(k)}(p)=2+\varphi^{(k)}(p). For k=2k=2 this gives φ⁡(p−1)=p−3\varphi(p-1)=p-3; since φ⁡(p−1)≤p−12\varphi(p-1)\leq\frac{p-1}{2} we get p≤5p\leq 5. For k≥3k\geq 3, Lemma 7.1 gives p−1≤2+p−12p-1\leq 2+\frac{p-1}{2}, again p≤5p\leq 5. Thus n∈{6,10}n\in\{6,10\}, and the table shows that 1010 is a solution for k=2k=2 only, while 66 never is. ∎

Remark 7.3.

The solution sets shrink from k=1k=1 to k=2k=2 and stabilise for all k≥3k\geq 3. The only solution lost between k=2k=2 and k=3k=3 is n=10n=10, because φ(3)​(5)=1<φ(2)​(5)=2\varphi^{(3)}(5)=1<\varphi^{(2)}(5)=2; the stabilisation reflects the fact that, for every prime p≥3p\geq 3, φ(2)​(p)=φ⁡(p−1)\varphi^{(2)}(p)=\varphi(p-1) is even, so the iterates beyond the second are at most half of it and the right-hand side of (7) can only reach φ⁡(n)\varphi(n) for the smallest values of nn. All three solution sets were confirmed by exhaustive computation up to 10510^{5} for k≤8k\leq 8.

The weighted form of (7), φ⁡(n)=c+α​∑p|nφ(k)​(p)\varphi(n)=c+\alpha\sum_{p\mid n}\varphi^{(k)}(p), behaves differently from the case k=1k=1 treated in §4: since φ(k)​(p)\varphi^{(k)}(p) is no longer linear in pp, the matched families of Theorem 4.2 disappear, but infinite families of a new, conditional kind appear. The simplest instance is the following.

Lemma 7.4.

Let p≥7p\geq 7 be a prime. Then φ⁡(p−1)=p−32\varphi(p-1)=\frac{p-3}{2} if and only if p−12\frac{p-1}{2} is prime, i.e. pp is a safe prime.

Proof.

Write p−1=2e​up-1=2^{e}u with uu odd, e≥1e\geq 1. Then φ⁡(p−1)=2e−1​φ​(u)\varphi(p-1)=2^{e-1}\varphi(u). If e≥2e\geq 2, then φ⁡(p−1)≤2e−1​u=p−12⋅φ⁡(u)u≤p−12\varphi(p-1)\leq 2^{e-1}u=\frac{p-1}{2}\cdot\frac{\varphi(u)}{u}\leq\frac{p-1}{2}, with φ⁡(p−1)=p−32\varphi(p-1)=\frac{p-3}{2} only if 2e−1​(u−φ⁡(u))=12^{e-1}(u-\varphi(u))=1, impossible for e≥2e\geq 2. So e=1e=1, p−1=2​up-1=2u, φ⁡(p−1)=φ⁡(u)\varphi(p-1)=\varphi(u), and φ⁡(u)=u−1\varphi(u)=u-1 holds if and only if u=p−12u=\frac{p-1}{2} is prime; since p≥7p\geq 7, u≥3u\geq 3 is odd. ∎

Proposition 7.5.

The composite solutions of φ⁡(n)=4​∑p|nφ(2)​(p)\varphi(n)=4\sum_{p\mid n}\varphi^{(2)}(p) are exactly

{8, 24, 60}∪{3p, 4p:psafe prime,p≥7}∪{6p:p=4q+1prime,qprime}.\{8,\,24,\,60\}\;\cup\;\{3p,\ 4p:\ p\ \text{safe prime},\ p\geq 7\}\;\cup\;\{6p:\ p=4q+1\ \text{prime},\ q\ \text{prime}\}.

In particular, the solution set is infinite if and only if there are infinitely many primes pp with p−12\frac{p-1}{2} or p−14\frac{p-1}{4} prime; under Dickson’s conjecture all three families are infinite.

Proof.

Let PP be the largest prime factor of nn and write n=m​Pan=mP^{a}, P∤mP\nmid m. If a≥2a\geq 2, the argument of Theorem 4.4 (case a≥2a\geq 2) applies verbatim, since φ(2)​(p)≤φ⁡(p)\varphi^{(2)}(p)\leq\varphi(p), and the resulting finite search gives only n=8n=8. Let a=1a=1 and m≥2m\geq 2. Writing Sm(2)=∑q|mφ⁡(q−1)S^{(2)}_{m}=\sum_{q\mid m}\varphi(q-1), the equation reads

φ⁡(m)​(P−1)= 4​Sm(2)+4​φ​(P−1).\varphi(m)(P-1)\;=\;4S^{(2)}_{m}+4\varphi(P-1).

Since φ⁡(P−1)≤P−12\varphi(P-1)\leq\frac{P-1}{2}, this gives φ⁡(m)≤2+4​Sm(2)P−1\varphi(m)\leq 2+\frac{4S^{(2)}_{m}}{P-1}. If φ⁡(m)≥4\varphi(m)\geq 4 then P−1≤2​Sm(2)≤2​∑q|m(q−2)P-1\leq 2S^{(2)}_{m}\leq 2\sum_{q\mid m}(q-2), which bounds PP in terms of mm while PP exceeds every prime factor of mm; the finitely many cases are n=24=8⋅3n=24=8\cdot 3 and n=60=12⋅5n=60=12\cdot 5, where equality φ⁡(m)=2+4​Sm(2)/(P−1)=4\varphi(m)=2+4S^{(2)}_{m}/(P-1)=4 holds. Otherwise φ⁡(m)=2\varphi(m)=2, i.e. m∈{3,4,6}m\in\{3,4,6\}. For m∈{3,4}m\in\{3,4\} one has Sm(2)=1S^{(2)}_{m}=1 and the equation becomes φ⁡(P−1)=P−32\varphi(P-1)=\frac{P-3}{2}, i.e. PP is a safe prime by Lemma 7.4 (and P≥7P\geq 7 since P>3P>3 and P=5P=5 fails). For m=6m=6, S6(2)=2S^{(2)}_{6}=2 and the equation becomes φ⁡(P−1)=P−52\varphi(P-1)=\frac{P-5}{2}; writing P−1=2e​uP-1=2^{e}u as in Lemma 7.4, this forces e=2e=2 and φ⁡(u)=u−1\varphi(u)=u-1, i.e. P=4​q+1P=4q+1 with qq prime. ∎

The sets were confirmed by exhaustive computation up to 2⋅1052\cdot 10^{5}: of the 10291029 composite solutions, 872872 are of the form 3​p3p or 4​p4p with pp safe, 154154 of the form 6​p6p with p=4​q+1p=4q+1, and 33 are sporadic. Thus, for k≥2k\geq 2, finiteness of the solution sets of the weighted iterated equation is not a theorem but is tied to the distribution of primes pp for which φ⁡(p−1)\varphi(p-1) is prescribed, a question of Sophie Germain type.

8 Numerical verification

All finite claims of this paper were verified by an exhaustive computation over 2≤n≤2⋅1052\leq n\leq 2\cdot 10^{5} using SymPy. The composite solution sets found were: {4,12,30}\{4,12,30\} for (Eφ)(E_{\varphi}), in agreement with [9]; {p2≤2⋅105}\{p^{2}\leq 2\cdot 10^{5}\} and nothing else for (Eτ)(E_{\tau}); the empty set for (Eσ)(E_{\sigma}), for J2J_{2}, for the weighted equation with (c,α)=(1,2)(c,\alpha)=(1,2), and for the triple system; and {4}\{4\} for the pair (Eφ)∧(Eτ)(E_{\varphi})\wedge(E_{\tau}). The expansion of Theorem 6.1 was compared with exact sieve computations up to x=107x=10^{7}, and the sporadic sets of Theorem 4.8 were obtained by the bounded mechanism enumeration of Lemma 4.7, independently cross-checked against the direct scan. The solution sets of Theorem 7.2 were checked for n≤105n\leq 10^{5} and 1≤k≤81\leq k\leq 8. The census of Theorem 4.12 was cross-checked against a direct scan of all composites n≤106n\leq 10^{6}, and the values |F⁡(c,1)||F(c,1)| for 1≤c≤20001\leq c\leq 2000 quoted in Question 9.2 were obtained by the bounded enumeration of Theorem 4.13(i)–(ii). The verification scripts are available from the authors.

9 Concluding remarks and open problems

The results assembled here suggest that the natural home of the Ranjan–Singh theorem is the family of prime–composite characterization problems, alongside Subbarao’s {4,6,22}\{4,6,22\} [10] and, in the unsolved direction, Lehmer’s problem [8]. We close with four problems.

Question 9.1.

Theorem 4.13 gives |F⁡(c,α)|≪L2​(log⁡L)2|F(c,\alpha)|\ll L^{2}(\log L)^{2} with L=|c|+αL=|c|+\alpha, whereas Theorem 4.12 gives |F⁡(c,α)|≤9|F(c,\alpha)|\leq 9 for L≤16L\leq 16, a direct scan of n≤2⋅106n\leq 2\cdot 10^{6} gives |F⁡(c,α)|≤19|F(c,\alpha)|\leq 19 for |c|≤40|c|\leq 40, α≤12\alpha\leq 12, and |F⁡(c,1)|≤9|F(c,1)|\leq 9 for all 1≤c≤20001\leq c\leq 2000. Is supc|F⁡(c,α)|\sup_{c}|F(c,\alpha)| finite for each fixed α\alpha? The maximizers observed, (6,6)(6,6), (12,4)(12,4), (40,8)(40,8), (27,9)(27,9), (36,12)(36,12), all satisfy α|c\alpha\mid c, as one expects from (5): when α\alpha divides cc and φ⁡(m′)\varphi(m^{\prime}), the divisibility obstruction in P−1=(c+α​Sm′)/(φ⁡(m′)−α)P-1=(c+\alpha S_{m^{\prime}})/(\varphi(m^{\prime})-\alpha) disappears. Is |F⁡(c,α)||F(c,\alpha)| governed by gcd⁡(c,α)\gcd(c,\alpha) and the divisor structure of α\alpha?

Question 9.2.

For α=1\alpha=1, equation (4) reads Δ⁡(n)=c−1\Delta(n)=c-1, with Δ\Delta the deficiency of §6, so that |F⁡(c,1)||F(c,1)| is the multiplicity of the value c−1c-1 of Δ\Delta on composite integers outside the family {2​p}\{2p\}, the analogue for Δ\Delta of the classical multiplicity problems for φ\varphi [6]. For 1≤c≤20001\leq c\leq 2000, F⁡(c,1)F(c,1) is empty for 341341 values of cc, the first being 6,12,22,23,24,30,42,46,60,726,12,22,23,24,30,42,46,60,72; the mean multiplicity is stable, close to 22; and every multiplicity 0,1,…,90,1,\dots,9 occurs, first at c=6,2,4,1,3,27,15,403,1047,943c=6,2,4,1,3,27,15,403,1047,943. Thus the analogue of Carmichael’s conjecture fails for Δ\Delta (F⁡(c,1)F(c,1) is a singleton for c=2,8,10c=2,8,10). Does every multiplicity occur, as Ford proved for φ\varphi? Does the set of cc with F⁡(c,1)=∅F(c,1)=\varnothing have positive density? Its parity bias is striking: it contains about 30%30\% of the even values of cc against 5%5\% of the odd ones, an even cc requiring an odd nn by Theorem 4.1(iii).

Question 9.3.

Theorem 7.2 settles the iterated equation with c=α=1c=\alpha=1, and Proposition 7.5 shows that for (c,α)=(0,4)(c,\alpha)=(0,4) and k=2k=2 the solution set is infinite if and only if there are infinitely many safe primes. Describe, for general (c,α)(c,\alpha) and k≥2k\geq 2, the conditional families of the weighted iterated equation φ⁡(n)=c+α​∑p|nφ(k)​(p)\varphi(n)=c+\alpha\sum_{p\mid n}\varphi^{(k)}(p): they are of the form {m​p}\{mp\} with φ⁡(m)≤α\varphi(m)\leq\alpha and pp subject to a condition φ(k−1)​(p−1)=ℓ​p+r\varphi^{(k-1)}(p-1)=\ell p+r, and one expects each of them to be infinite under Dickson’s conjecture.

Question 9.4.

Theorem 6.1 describes the average of Δ⁡(n)\Delta(n). Determine the distribution of Δ⁡(n)/φ⁡(n)\Delta(n)/\varphi(n), which is expected to tend to 11 in mean.

Finally, apart from the squares of primes (OEIS A001248), none of the solution sets occurring here, in particular {4,12,30}\{4,12,30\}, appears to be catalogued in the OEIS at the time of writing; submitting them would usefully anchor the problem in the literature.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
